author: Anele Mbi
title: Buffalo City’s broken houses and decades of empty promises
content:
A housing rectification project in Braelyn Extension 10 in Buffalo City Municipality (BCM) has left residents frustrated with the municipality’s failure to address severe structural faults.




Serious defects in the RD houses include cracked walls and roofs, leaking roofs, and inadequate foundations. Braelyn residents say they have repeatedly complained to the municipality, which has promised to rebuild the houses since 2004, but has taken no action until today, except for a laydown yard constructed by the sitting, ANC ward councillor, Mendi Wetsetse.




The stalled housing project intersects with service-delivery defects across the ward, including unpaved and potholed roads, poor refuse collection, and electricity shortages brought about by the growing Inkandla informal settlement.




Recently, President Cyril Ramaphosa authorised the Special Investigating Unit (SIU) to probe allegations of extensive corruption and maladministration of major BCM tenders.




According to Braelyn residents, talks about rectifying Braelyn Ext 10 RDP houses began before 2010. The then ward councillor, Thabo Myira, who served as a councillor between 2005 and 2010, confirmed the claim.




Media reports also indicate that in 2009, the then minister of human settlements, Tokyo Sexwale promised people living in faulty RDP houses in East London that their houses would be rebuilt. Today, councillor Wetsetse, who is campaigning for a third term in the upcoming local government election, promised to rectify the situation.




Housing defects




Ntombizanele Mabala, an 80-year-old pensioner, said since residents arrived in Braelyn in 1997, they have complained to councillors and the municipality about the poor condition of their houses, but their pleas were ignored. “These are not houses but hokkies. We have children and a family of six. Rain comes in from every direction – through the roof, the walls and underneath – because these houses have no foundations,” she said. “The councillor promised that the housing rectification process would begin before 4 November, but there are still no signs of work apart from a laydown-yard fence erected two years ago.”




Another pensioner, Nothembile Mqhayi, whose house was built below ground level, said her house floods when it rains. She showed 

Elitsha

 a hole she had made at the bottom of a wall to let water that entered the house drain out.




The Mqhayi family had to make a hole in the wall to drain out water when the house floods.




Ziyanda Mpakantsho (42), who recently joined an EPWP project and earns R3,000 a month, said rectification is urgently needed because she lives with a sick and disabled person. “I grew up hearing that the cracks in the walls would be repaired, but many years have passed. These Braelyn houses have no proper foundations, so water leaks in when it rains. The houses have not been rectified because the money is being squandered,” she said.




Zama Thutha (70) said the government had not fixed the RDP houses because it was corrupt and unaccountable to voters. “Even the EPWP jobs created recently will end after the elections. Our system of government is capitalism, which puts profit before the needs of ordinary people,” he said.




Recurring delays and more promises




Responses from both the BCM and the Eastern Cape department of human settlements (DHS) are not only conflicting but also suggest the rectification process remains a false hope for Braelyn residents. When asked whether the municipality or its ward councillor has made any promises of rectification, the municipality said the provincial government is responsible for the rectification process.




“The Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality wishes to clarify that it does not currently run a municipal housing rectification programme; this falls outside local government funding allocations. What we can say is that the laydown yard established on-site remains a site-securing measure for future development once capital is allocated.”




The laydown yard is overgrown

.




The provincial DHS said that, despite the constitutional principle of cooperative governance that compels the various spheres of government to share information and support each other, implementation requires compliance with the necessary technical, administrative, planning, and budgetary processes. The department has not denied the fact that rectification has been recognised for several years.




“The programme, which focuses on the rectification of existing two-room RDP houses, was prioritised following engagements involving the current ward councillor and the executive mayor of BCMM,” said Yanga Funani, the DHS spokesperson.




“In the current financial year, Braelyn, Ducats and Dimbaza have been identified among the priority areas for rectification,” said Funani. “The project is currently at an advanced preparatory stage, with implementation targeted to commence in November 2026, subject to the completion of outstanding administrative and implementation requirements,” he added.

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu to campaign for ANC and SACP
content:
Cosatu has pledged to campaign for both the African National Congress (ANC) and the South African Communist Party (SACP) in the upcoming local government elections, warning that its political support will not prevent it from confronting either party if workers’ interests are undermined.




SACP candidates will be contesting the local government polls on 4 November, independently of the ANC for the first time since 1994. 




The position emerged from the federation’s 15

th

 national congress, which was held from 12 to 14 October after its 

first attempt in September collapsed

. In her first formal press statement as the newly elected general secretary, Zingiswa Losi said the congress reaffirmed Cosatu’s historic mission to organise and mobilise the working class, defend workers’ rights and advance a programme of democratic transformation towards socialism.




The federation’s decision to support both the ANC and SACP followed consultations among affiliates. Losi explained that the unions had adopted positions intended to influence the national congress, which ultimately passed what the leadership called a “super resolution” to support both parties.




The motion to back the SACP was championed by one of Cosatu’s largest affiliates, the National Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu). Losi defended Nehawu and the right of affiliates to consult their constituencies and bring their positions to the congress. She maintained that they had not acted improperly and that the decisive outcome was the congress’s collective resolution supporting both the ANC and SACP. Cosatu’s demands regarding local government, labour rights and public services would apply to both parties. she said. 




Congress resolutions




The agenda of Cosatu’s congress involved discussions on the future of organised labour amid mass unemployment, poverty, inequality and rising living costs. The congress acknowledged the need to rebuild Cosatu’s organisational strength and reverse the trend of declining membership in parts of the private sector. 




Cosatu’s declared priority is to rebuild workplace structures, organise un-unionised and precariously employed workers, strengthen collective bargaining and to improve accountability among affiliates.




One of the federation’s key proposals is a workers’ cost-of-living index to inform wage negotiations and government policy. Losi argued that economic progress should not be measured simply by declining inflation or headline growth, but by whether workers and their families could afford to live with dignity. “What it costs for workers to live must inform the bargaining strategy,” she said.




The proposed index would assess the weight of food, transport, electricity and healthcare costs on household budgets. Cosatu wants wage negotiations to take into account what money workers have left after meeting essential expenses, particularly when salary increases fail to keep pace with inflation.




The federation is also calling for an expanded basket of zero-rated goods, affordable basic services and the implementation of National Health Insurance to ease the cost of medical care.




Cosatu urged consumers and government to support locally produced goods, arguing that stronger domestic production can help protect manufacturing jobs. The federation maintains that economic growth must translate into employment and improved living standards rather than leave workers trapped in poverty.




Cosatu’s general secretary, Zingiswa Losi campaigning for the ANC in Khayelitsha recently. Photo from Zingiswa Losi’s Facebook page




Cosatu criticises the composition of GNU




While continuing to support the ANC, Cosatu still criticised the composition of the government of national unity, particularly the inclusion of the Democratic Alliance, citing differences over policies such as national health insurance and the national minimum wage. The federation argued that rebuilding the tri-partite alliance with the ANC and SACP must not require workers to accept policies that undermine their interests.




Newly elected president, Mike Shingange stressed that Cosatu’s electoral support was not unconditional. “It doesn’t mean when we campaign and vote for you, and you undermine the interests of the workers, that we’re not going to come for you. We will,” he said.




Shingange said Cosatu would not remain silent if either political partner failed to honour commitments to workers. He warned that their conduct in government could influence the federation’s future political support, although he did not specify what concrete political sanction would follow.




He said the federation would continue defending workers through collective bargaining, workplace representation, legal processes and public mobilisation.

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Multi-million rand sports facility finally opens in Limpopo
content:
Finally, Waterval residents in Limpopo outside of Elim Hospital are now able to utilise their R55-million sports facility having waited for over a decade of delays. The Waterval facility is not the only one that has been neglected by Limpopo municipalities. Earlier this year, 

Elitsha 

reported on the R1.4-million upgrades to 

Makwarela Stadium

 that never happened.




How it all started




The Waterval sports facility, which consists of a soccer field and a tennis court, was officially handed over to the Waterval community earlier this month. This came as welcome relief to local residents who had already lost hope that the facility would ever open. At one stage, it was left abandoned and turned into a drug den and a hiding place for criminals.




The facility is set to be utilised for various sporting codes by the local communities and schools. “At last, our children have got a ground where they can play their football with ease. Even though we had to wait for years for the facility to be completed, we are happy now that the ground is ours. To be honest, I am one of the people who had already lost hope that one day, the facility will ever be used for our benefit,” says Cedric Mulaudzi, a resident of Waterval.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Austerity under fire as Godongwana pauses fuel levies and low-cost housing
content:
Residents, activists, members of trade unions and civil society groups took to the streets of Cape Town earlier today against budget cuts. This was before the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement was delivered by the Minister of Finance, Enoch Godongwana. Led by Cry of the Xcluded, some of the protesters’ demands included the right to decent work, an end to exclusionary access to free basic services, an end to privatisation, an increase in health, education and policing, and an universal basic income amongst others.




Equal Education’s secretary general, Itumeleng Mothlabane said that the budget cuts in education have resulted in the existence of plain pit latrines in schools, overcrowded classrooms and learners having to walk on dangerous roads when they go to school.




“We reject a budget that continues to deprioritise the education of a poor black learner. We demand an increase in the allocation that is given to each and every learner. We demand an increase in the school infrastructure budget in Limpopo, KwaZulu-Natal, the Eastern Cape and all the rural provinces,” Mothlabane said.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘End hunger, stop climate harm’: protesters take demands to Parliament
content:
About 200 residents and activists marched through the streets of Cape Town on World Food Day, calling for the government to end hunger and stop climate harm. Organised by the Climate Justice Charter Movement (CJCM) and the South African Food Sovereignty Campaign and allied partners, the protesters handed the memorandum to parliament where they called for the adoption of the People’s Sovereignty Act No 1 of 2024, a People’s Sovereignty Policy and an immediate ban on pesticides.




At least 14 to 15 million people in South Africa live below the food poverty line and experience regular food insecurity, while 11,000 children die due to malnutrition every year, and 10-million tonnes of food go to waste every year, according to Unite Against Hunger. 




A recent report by the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food) found that nearly 1.4-billion people in the world work in the agrifood sector, including farmworkers. Despite their number and the vital role they play, they are among the most exploited workers in the world.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.




One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service. 




Speaking to 

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Make the wealthy pay: AIDC lays out alternative to austerity
content:
The potential to raise revenue by taxing wealth and high-income earners, rather than relying on spending cuts and taxes that place a greater burden on the poor, is massive according to a new report by the Alternative Information and Development Centre (AIDC).




AIDC held a tax justice workshop in Johannesburg on Friday, bringing together activists, labour representatives and civil society organisations to discuss alternatives to 

austerity

 and a progressive tax system.




Presenting the report, Chloé van Biljon, AIDC’s tax justice project officer, said the country’s persistent unemployment, poverty, inequality and economic stagnation requires the state to mobilise more resources for public services, social protection and industrial development. “The state needs to not only maintain the current level of public services and social support but has to expand them to deal with these problems,” van Biljon said.




One of the report’s proposals is to abolish the medical aid tax credit, which costs the state about R30-billion a year, and redirect the money towards social protection, including the Social Relief of Distress (SRD) grant. For the state to continue providing such a benefit to medical aid members while millions of poorer South Africans rely on limited social assistance, cannot be justified.
